ideas: One-sentence summary: the problem, the users, your role
How it works, at the level the interviewer wants
A key decision, the result, what you'd improve

phrases.meaning: STAR: says what you were responsible for

learn.explain: "Walk me through" questions test whether you really understand your own work and whether you can structure a technical explanation for different listeners. Start with a one-sentence summary: the problem, the users, and your role. Then give a high-level picture of how it works, the main parts and how data flows, before any details. Choose one important decision, explain the trade-off you made, and give the result. Stop after about two minutes and offer to go deeper, so the interviewer can steer. Watch their reaction and adjust the level: an engineering interviewer may want architecture details, a hiring manager wants impact.
points: One-sentence summary first: problem, users, your role.
Big picture before details; one key decision with its trade-off.
Stop and offer to go deeper; let the interviewer steer.
mistakes: Starting with the tech stack instead of the problem.
Talking for five minutes without checking if the level is right.
Not being able to explain a decision when asked "why?".

framework.starter: In a nutshell, it's a … that helps … to …
At a high level, it has three parts…
The main trade-off was… so what I did was…
I'm happy to go deeper into any part.

betterWays.strong: In a nutshell, it's a dashboard that helps the operations team find late deliveries before customers complain.
betterWays.why: Problem and users first; the stack can come later.

betterWays.weak: First the user open the page and then…
betterWays.strong: At a high level, it has three parts: data import, the delivery status logic, and the dashboard.

betterWays.strong: We chose Postgres over a NoSQL database because the data was very relational and the team already knew it.
I'm happy to go deeper into any part, maybe the data import, which was the trickiest.

betterWays.strong: As a result, late deliveries were spotted on average three hours earlier.

model: Sure. In a nutshell, it's a dashboard that helps a logistics company's operations team find late deliveries before customers complain. The situation was that the team tracked around two thousand deliveries a day in shared spreadsheets, updated by hand from three different systems. My role was building the backend and part of the frontend, during a six-month internship. At a high level, it has three parts. First, an import job that pulls delivery updates from the three systems every five minutes. Second, the status logic, which decides if a delivery is on time, at risk, or late, based on distance and the driver's current position. And third, the dashboard itself, which shows the at-risk list first. The main trade-off was in the import. Real-time updates would have been nicer, but one of the systems only offered file exports. So what I did was choose a five-minute schedule for all three, which kept the design simple and consistent, and I made the dashboard show when each source was last updated, so nobody was misled. As a result, late deliveries were spotted about three hours earlier on average, and the team stopped two hours of manual updates a day. I'm happy to go deeper into any part; the import was probably the trickiest.
short: In a nutshell, it's a dashboard that helps a logistics operations team find late deliveries early. It has three parts: an import job pulling from three systems, the status logic, and the dashboard. The main trade-off: one system only had file exports, so I used a simple five-minute schedule for all of them. As a result, delays were spotted three hours earlier.

followUps.q: How did you handle it when one of the source systems was down?
followUps.answer: The import for each source ran separately, so one failure didn't stop the others. The dashboard showed a warning with the time of the last successful update for that source, and the job retried a few times before alerting us.

followUps.q: How did you decide what counts as "at risk"?
followUps.answer: I didn't decide alone. I sat with two operators and asked how they judged it in their heads. Their rule was roughly: if the remaining distance can't be covered by the promised time at normal speed. I turned that into code and we tuned it together over two weeks.
I'd add automated tests around the status logic much earlier. We had a bug where deliveries crossing midnight were marked late, and a few simple tests would have caught it before the operators did.

selfCheck: I started with a one-sentence summary.
I gave the big picture before details.
I explained one decision and its trade-off.
I gave a result and offered to go deeper.
I answered the follow-up without restarting a sentence.
